questions.q: In the decision framework this lesson lays out, which factor should be checked first?
options: Which cloud has the cheapest published list price
Which cloud the team personally prefers
Compliance and data-residency requirements, because they can eliminate options outright regardless of cost or preference
Which cloud was used for the most recent workload
questions.explain: Hard constraints like data residency and sovereignty come first because they are non-negotiable — a cheaper or more familiar option is irrelevant if it legally or physically cannot host the data.

questions.q: What is the purpose of checking 'required services' as the second step, according to this lesson?
options: To rank every candidate cloud on a numeric score
To decide which team will operate the workload
To determine the workload's compliance requirements
To act as a yes/no filter: if a workload's required service doesn't exist (or has no equivalent) on a candidate cloud, that candidate is eliminated
questions.explain: This step is described as a yes/no filter, not a scoring exercise — a candidate cloud is removed from consideration if the workload's required service simply isn't available there.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say cost should be evaluated using 'effective cost' rather than published list price?
options: Because effective cost reflects the organization's actual, discount-adjusted pricing from existing commitments, which list price doesn't capture
Because list price is always higher than effective cost on every cloud
Because effective cost ignores all committed-use discounts
Because published list prices are classified information
questions.explain: An organization's existing commitments and discounts (amortized, as covered in Lesson 25) determine what a workload would really cost there, which published list price does not reflect.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat landing a workload on a cloud the team doesn't operate well as a real risk, separate from the invoice?
options: Because unfamiliar platforms always cost more on paper
Because operational risk from unfamiliarity exists independently of cost, and affects how safely and quickly the workload ships and runs
Because every cloud provider requires identical skills to operate
Because skill only matters for on-prem workloads, not cloud workloads
questions.explain: A team that runs a given cloud confidently will ship and operate a workload there faster and more safely than its first attempt on an unfamiliar platform, independent of what either option costs.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as the default placement for a new workload, absent a specific reason to do otherwise?
options: Whichever cloud currently has the lowest list price that week
Always split every workload evenly across both clouds
The cloud the organization already runs similar workloads on, treating multi-cloud placement as a deliberate exception rather than a default
Always place it on-prem first, then migrate later
questions.explain: The honest default is to land new workloads where similar workloads already run; multi-cloud placement should be chosen for a specific, named reason (a hard constraint or a genuine best-of-breed case), not applied by default.
